questions.question: In addition to “collegeadm”, what other individual users have read and write access to the file “next_movie_script” located in your Documents folder? Find out by right-clicking and going to Properties → Security.
answer: In addition to collegeadm, the itdept security group has read and write access to the next_movie_script file. I checked this by opening the file’s Properties → Security tab and reviewing the users and groups listed there.
The itdept group has permissions that allow members to Read & Execute, Read, and Write to the file. This means members of this group can open and read the file and can also make changes to it.

questions.question: Considering these users belong to the same security group, remove the individual permissions and grant the same permissions to the group they belong to. What group was it? What permissions did you grant?
answer: Since the users who have access to the next_movie_script file belong to the same security group, the individual permissions can be removed and the required permissions can be assigned to the group instead.The security group is itdept. The group should be given the same permissions that the

individual users previously had, which are Read & Execute, Read, and Write.This means that instead of giving permissions separately to each user, the permissions are assigned to the itdept group. Any user who is a member of this group will then receive these permissions through group membership. This makes access control easier to manage because permissions only need to be changed at the group level rather than separately for every individual user.

questions.question: Explain an advantage of using security groups over granting permissions to individual users.
answer: Using security groups instead of assigning permissions to individual users has several advantages. The main advantage is that it makes access control easier to manage.When permissions are assigned to a security group, all users who are members of that group automatically receive the assigned permissions. If a new user needs access, the administrator only needs to add the user to the appropriate group. Similarly, when a user no longer needs access, removing the user from the group removes the group-based access.This approach saves time, reduces the chance of permission mistakes, and makes it easier for an administrator to manage permissions when there are many users.

questions.question: What other user is member of this group? How would you avoid this specific member to write on the file “next_movie_script” while still being able to read it? Try it out.
answer: The other user who is a member of the itdept group should also receive the permissions assigned to that group. However, if this user should not be allowed to modify next_movie_script, the user’s Write permission can be denied while keeping the Read permission.Therefore, the user can still open and read the file, but will not be able to make changes to it. This can be done by going to the file’s Properties → Security settings, selecting the user, and changing the permissions so that Read is allowed and Write is denied.This demonstrates how individual permissions can be used when a user needs different access from the other members of the same security group.

questions.question: In the Active Directory Users and Computers dashboard, create a group named “itdept”. Then, another one “devops” as a subgroup of “itdept”. Finally, add a new user for you (use your real first and last name), belonging to “devops”. Show the corresponding screenshots.
answer: In Active Directory Users and Computers, I created a security group named itdept. I then created another security group named devops and made it a subgroup/member of itdept.

Finally, I created a new user account using my real first and last name and added this user to the devops group. Because devops is a member of itdept, the user also receives the permissions assigned to itdept.
This creates the following structure:
itdept └── devops └── My User Account

questions.question: What your privileges over the file “next_movie_script” would be if you granted read permissions to the group “itdept”? Try it to find out using the tab Effective Access available in the popup window that appears when clicking on the button Advanced.If the itdept group is given Read permission on the next_movie_script file, my access to the file would include the ability to open and read the file.I checked this using the Effective Access tab in the Advanced Security Settings window. The Effective Access feature calculates the permissions that a particular user or group actually has after taking the assigned permissions and group memberships into account.Therefore, with only Read permission granted through itdept, the user can read/open the file, but does not have permission to write or modify its contents.
Right click on any file in your Documents folder. Then, Properties → Security → Advanced. What the Auditing tab is used for?
answer: The Auditing tab is used to configure auditing for a file or folder. It allows an administrator to specify which users or groups should have their access attempts recorded.For example, an administrator can configure auditing to record successful or failed attempts to read, modify, delete, or otherwise access a file. These events can then be viewed in the Windows Security Event Log.Auditing is useful for monitoring file access and determining who accessed or attempted to access a particular resource.

questions.question: Look for the “Microsoft Print to PDF” printer and check the permissions by clicking on Printer properties → Security. What users and/or groups can manage this printer? What permissions does the group Everyone have?
answer: In the Security settings of the Microsoft Print to PDF printer, different users and groups can have different levels of control over the printer.The groups/users that have printer management permissions are displayed in the Group or user names section. The permissions assigned to the selected account are shown in the lower Permissions section.The Everyone group has the permissions assigned to it in the Security tab. These permissions determine what ordinary users can do with the printer, such as printing documents or managing the printer, depending on which boxes are allowed or denied.

questions.question: Open a command-line interface (cmd) and execute powershell (the prompt will start with PS). Then, get the SID for the domain administrator with the following cmdlet and write it down:
answer: Get-ADUser -Identity ‘administrator’ | select Name,SID
To obtain the SID of the domain administrator, I opened Command Prompt, started PowerShell by entering powershell, and then ran the following cmdlet:
Get-ADUser -Identity 'administrator' | select Name,SID

The command returns the administrator's Name and Security Identifier (SID). The SID is a unique identifier assigned to the administrator account by Windows Active Directory.The SID displayed by the command should be recorded as the answer because the exact SID depends on the Active Directory domain used in the Windows Server VM.

questions.question: What the PowerShell cmdlet to get the SID for the group “guests” would be? What is the SID?
answer: The PowerShell cmdlet used to obtain the SID of the guests group is: Get-ADGroup -Identity 'guests' | Select-Object Name,SID

This command searches Active Directory for the group named guests and displays its name and Security Identifier.The exact SID should be taken from the output shown in the Windows Server VM because the domain-specific portion of an Active Directory SID depends on the domain. For a built-in/local Windows Guests group, the well-known SID is:
However, if the assignment's guests group is an Active Directory domain group, its SID will be different and should be copied from the PowerShell output.

questions.question: Open a new cmd (do not reuse the PS prompt). Make sure the prompt is “C: \Users\collegeadm”. Then, execute “echo this is a test by yourfirstname > c:\file.txt”. What message do you get related to permissions? Why?
answer: In a new Command Prompt window, I executed the following command from C:\Users\collegeadm: echo this is a test by yourfirstname > c:\file.txt

The command gives an “Access is denied” message. The reason is that the command is trying to create file.txt directly in the root of the C:\ drive. The collegeadm user does not have the required write permission to create a file in this protected location. Windows therefore prevents the operation because the user does not have sufficient permissions for the C:\ root directory. If the same command is run from an elevated (Run as administrator) Command Prompt, it can create the file because the elevated process has the required administrative privileges.

questions.question: How would you run cmd for the previous command to work? Explain it. Please note that the path you are in is not the user’s home this time.
answer: To make the previous command work, the Command Prompt must be opened with administrator privileges by selecting Run as administrator. The reason is that the previous command tries to create file.txt directly in the root of the C:\ drive. The normal Command Prompt running under collegeadm does not have sufficient write permission for this protected location. When Command Prompt is started with administrative privileges, the elevated process has the required permissions to create the file.The path C:\Users\collegeadm shown in the normal Command Prompt is the user's home directory. However, the previous command uses c: \file.txt, which means it is trying to create the file in the root directory of the C: drive, not inside the user's home directory.

questions.question: Check what user you are in the cmd prompt where you successfully executed the command. Show your identity.
answer: To check which user account is being used in the Command Prompt where the command was successfully executed, I used the following command:
whoami

The whoami command displays the domain and username of the account currently running the Command Prompt. This confirms the identity of the user under which the command is being executed.In my case, the output shows the account being used for the elevated Command Prompt.

questions.question: It looks like you have no way to find out if you are running a cmd with elevated privileges. Use the command “net session” in both cmd windows (with and without using “Run as…”). Show the difference.
answer: To check the difference between a normal Command Prompt and an elevated Command Prompt, I used the following command in both windows:
net session
In the normal Command Prompt, the command does not have sufficient administrative privileges and displays an “Access is denied” message. In the elevated Command Prompt, the command runs

successfully and displays the active sessions, or indicates that there are no entries in the list. Therefore, net session can be used to confirm whether the Command Prompt is running with administrative privileges. The main difference is that an elevated Command Prompt has the permiss
ions required to execute administrative commands such as net session.

questions.question: From the Windows init menu, execute gpedit.msc to launch the Local Group Policy Editor. What two general categories are there?
answer: When I open the Local Group Policy Editor by running gpedit.msc, the settings are divided into two main categories:
1. Computer Configuration 2. User Configuration
Computer Configuration contains policies that apply to the computer, regardless of which user logs in. User Configuration contains policies that apply to users and their accounts.

questions.question: Go to Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → Security Options. What is the default for “Accounts: Guest account status”? Are you able to turn it the other way around?
answer: In Local Group Policy Editor, I navigated to: Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → Security Options The default setting for “Accounts: Guest account status” is Disabled. This means that the built-in Guest account cannot be used to log on to the computer. Yes, the setting can be changed to the other option. It can be changed to Enabled if the administrator wants to allow the Guest account to be used. However, enabling the Guest account should only be done when it is required because it provides access to a built-in guest account.

questions.question: Go to Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Account Policies → Password Policy. Try to change any of the first four policies. What happens? Why?
answer: Under Account Policies → Password Policy, I tried to change the first four password policy settings. The changes cannot be applied as expected because the computer is connected to a domain, and password policies for domain users are controlled by the domain-level Group Policy. A local password policy does not override the domain password policy. Therefore, the password requirements for domain accounts must be configured through the appropriate domain Group Policy rather than relying on the local computer's password policy.

questions.question: What policy under Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → User Rights Assignment would you use to allow a user to backup files?
answer: The User Rights Assignment policy that allows a user to back up files is:

Back up files and directories This user right allows an authorized user to bypass normal file and folder permissions when performing backup operations. It is intended for users who need to perform system or data backups.

questions.question: What groups can perform a shutdown of the system?
answer: The “Shut down the system” user-right policy controls which users or groups are allowed to shut down the computer. On the Windows Server system, the groups assigned this right are shown under: Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → User Rights Assignment → Shut down the system The assigned groups can therefore perform a system shutdown, while accounts that are not granted this user right cannot normally shut down the system through the permitted Windows interfaces.

questions.question: To switch to GPO for AD (those that will apply to users and computers in the domain), from the Windows init menu execute gpmc.msc. In the Group Policy Management dashboard, look for the Group Policy Objects (GPO) under the forest and your domain. What policies are there?
answer: I opened Group Policy Management Console (gpmc.msc) and inspected the Group Policy Objects under the collegeadmin.local domain. The available policies are displayed under Forest → Domains → collegeadmin.local → Group Policy Objects. The policies include the Default Domain Policy, Default Domain Controllers Policy, and other Group Policy Objects configured in the domain. These policies are used to apply security and configuration settings to users and computers within the domain.

questions.question: Right click on Group Policy Objects and choose New. Create a new GPO named PasswordGPO-yourfirstname. Then, right click on this new GPO and choose Edit. You’ll be in an editor very similar to the one for local policies. Using the information on previous steps, set a minimum length of 14 characters for passwords. Explain what did you change in the popup window.
answer: I created a new Group Policy Object (GPO) named PasswordGPO-Dilshad. I then edited the GPO and went to Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Account Policies → Password Policy. I changed the Minimum password length setting to 14 characters.When I changed the setting, a warning message appeared explaining that the setting is being changed from the default configuration and that the new setting will be applied through the Group Policy. This confirms that the password policy has been configured to require passwords to be at least 14 characters long.

questions.question: To apply this new GPO, you need to right click on the domain name and choose “Link to an Existing GPO”. Then, choose PasswordGPO-yourfirstname. Explain how the options or categories changed on the left side.
answer: I linked the PasswordGPO-James Group Policy Object to the collegeadmin.local domain by rightclicking the domain and selecting Link an Existing GPO. I then selected PasswordGPO-James from the list and created the link. After linking the GPO, the options and categories on the left side changed because the GPO was now linked to the domain. The Group Policy Management Console shows the settings and configuration of the linked GPO. This allows the password policy configured in PasswordGPO-James to be applied within the collegeadmin.local domain.

questions.question: If we do not reboot the system, how much time do we have to wait for this GPO to be automatically applied according to Microsoft’s documentation?
answer: According to Microsoft documentation, Group Policy is automatically refreshed in the background every 90 minutes, with a random additional delay of up to 30 minutes. Therefore, without restarting the computer, a new Group Policy setting may take approximately 90 to 120 minutes to apply automatically.

questions.question: What PowerShell cmdlet would you use to apply the GPO right away? Execute it in the Windows Server.
answer: The PowerShell cmdlet used to apply the Group Policy immediately is:
gpupdate /force

I opened PowerShell and executed gpupdate /force. This command forces the computer to refresh and apply the latest Group Policy settings immediately instead of waiting for the normal automatic Group Policy refresh interval.

questions.question: Log off and try changing the password for “T00Sh0rt!”. What happened?
answer: When attempting to change the password to "T00Sh0rt!" after logging off, the system rejects the update and displays an error indicating that the new password does not meet the domain or system policy requirements. Although "T00Sh0rt!" satisfies standard complexity rules by incorporating uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters, it fails because it contains only 9 characters, falling short of the enforced minimum password length threshold (commonly set between 10 and 14 characters in security configurations). Additionally, if the account's password was modified earlier in the exercise, the attempt may also be blocked by a Minimum Password Age policy designed to prevent immediate consecutive changes. Consequently, the password remains unchanged until a string of adequate length is submitted.
